115	# File Links
116	
117	## Guidance
118	
119	When a reader-visible response refers to a local file, use a Markdown link: `[Description](target)`. The description
120	must contain the target's filename and, when available, append a colon followed by its decimal line number, such as
121	`ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7`. When the response refers to different targets with the same filename, include the
122	smallest subset of each target's full path that lets the reader distinguish them; otherwise do not include a directory
123	in the description. The target may use the full available path. Before finalizing, reject a bracketed local-file label
124	such as `[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7]` unless it has the Markdown link target required by this rule; brackets alone
125	are not a link. Write the target immediately after `(` and before `)`, without leading or trailing whitespace.
126

128	# Intermediate versus Terminal Goals
129	
130	## Guidance
131	
132	For every workflow, name the terminal goal and the acceptance evidence that proves it. Classify plans, staging
133	artifacts, repairs, migrations, investigations, commits, recorded transitions, and verification as intermediate tasks
134	unless their evidence proves every terminal acceptance condition.
135	
136	Record every required terminal gate and its required evidence before execution. Mark each gate passed, failed, unrun, or
137	explicitly excluded by the user; do not infer a passed state from a related check. A failed or unrun required gate is an
138	unmet terminal condition. A clean build, an inspected result, a repaired intermediate artifact, or an existing sequence
139	of commits cannot substitute for the gate that the workflow requires.
140	
141	Match evidence to the claim each terminal gate makes. Evidence that establishes only an enabling condition—such as
142	installation, configuration, authorization, discovery, connection, initialization, or process start—may pass only an
143	availability gate. It cannot pass a behavior or outcome gate. For those gates, require evidence from the relevant
144	execution boundary that the required behavior ran and produced its required effect. When availability itself is the
145	terminal outcome, record availability as that gate's claim.
146	
147	When new work arises, classify it before acting. It supports the current terminal goal unless the user explicitly
148	replaces or expands that goal. Record its own completion evidence separately. After it completes, re-evaluate the
149	unchanged terminal conditions and continue from the next unmet condition. Do not report completion, return control as
150	complete, or discard required follow-up work on intermediate evidence.
151	
152	Treat a user instruction as a goal change only when it explicitly replaces or expands the requested terminal outcome. A
153	discovered prerequisite, failure, repair, workaround, or implementation detail does not change that outcome merely
154	because completing it is necessary to proceed.
155	
156	Before an irreversible action that represents completion—such as committing, finalizing, publishing, or declaring a
157	workflow complete—record the user-authorized scope and compare it with terminal acceptance evidence. Every scoped item
158	must have completion evidence or an explicit user-authorized exclusion. A prior result may reduce the remaining scope
159	only when durable evidence proves it covered the same item under the same governing contract; a tidy-looking history, an
160	earlier status claim, or partial inspection is intermediate evidence, not proof. Otherwise continue across the full
161	authorized scope. Immediately before the terminal action or claim, repeat that comparison, including the recorded gate
162	states, and report remaining work instead of success when any item is unaccounted for or any required gate is failed or
163	unrun.
164	
165	---
166	# Target Audience
167	
168	## Guidance
169	
170	Write every user response, prompt or rule file, source comment or Javadoc, command help text, and error message so its
171	intended reader can identify the relevant actor, input or state, action, result, and next decision without knowing this
172	project's vocabulary.
173	
174	Prefer common precise language. Introduce a specialized or abstract workflow term only when it conveys a distinction
175	that common language loses; define it at its first reader-visible use in concrete terms. Do not define a term by
176	repeating it or replacing it with other undefined project terms. When a plain definition still needs workflow
177	vocabulary, add the shortest before-to-after example that shows the ordinary observable effect. For example, replace
178	“whole later correction commit” with “a later commit containing only changes that complete or correct one earlier
179	feature.”
180	
181	Apply the same test to a new category, exception, boundary, or conclusion. It is unexplained when a reader must accept a
182	label such as “family”, “complete”, or “required” without being told which observable facts make it true and what
183	decision those facts require. Do not let an example or desired result define that boundary. At its first use, name the
184	actor, observable facts, acceptance evidence, and resulting decision; then check one meaningful analogous case and one
185	dissimilar case to ensure the wording states the shared condition rather than the example's label.
186	
187	Do not use an internal state or compound relationship label as its own explanation in reader-facing prose. Name the
188	artifact or action it represents and why it matters. When the label conceals why an operation cannot work in a receiving
189	state, explain the smallest causal sequence before proposing a remedy: the original and receiving states, operation,
190	assumption missing from the receiving state, and observable result. Then create a version of the selected operation that
191	relies only on the receiving state and verify its intended result. When the workflow lacks that capability, say that the
192	workflow and tool need a feature to create and verify it; do not imply that the change is impossible.
193	
194	When warning that a check, observation, or result cannot establish a conclusion, explain the failed reasoning as an
195	observable sequence. Name the check or observation, the conclusion it might lead the reader to draw, the inputs or cases
196	it leaves unexamined, and the resulting incorrect decision. Then state the replacement procedure: which artifacts or
197	inputs to examine, the comparison or decision to make, and the evidence that completes it. Do not say only that the
198	reader must not rely on, assume, or treat something as proof; that does not explain why it is insufficient or how to
199	obtain the missing evidence.
200	
201	When explaining a diagnosis, do not replace observed evidence and its limited conclusion with an internal label such as
202	"the model-facing boundary." First name the producer, the artifact, the differing observed values, and the resulting
203	behavior in their causal order. Then state only what those observations establish. If the unobserved step that changes a
204	value is not yet known, say that it remains to be located and name the next check; do not assign it to a component merely
205	because it lies between two observations.
206	
207	For example, a patch prepared after `addsValidation()` exists can rely on that unchanged nearby text. When an earlier
208	commit lacks the method, Git cannot locate the patch. Create a version relative to that earlier commit and verify it. Do
209	not lead with labels such as “source tree,” “destination tree,” “target-adapted,” “reconstruction,” or “context” unless
210	the reader has first been given this explanation or the term is immediately defined in it.
211	
212	Do not explain ordinary, broadly understood technical terms unless the project gives them a specialized meaning.
213	
214	Before finalizing prose, review the actual draft—not only these guidelines—for internal labels, compound relationship
215	labels, and unexplained workflow terms. For each one, either replace it with the concrete artifact, relationship, and
216	action it hides, or define it where it first appears. Then ask whether the intended reader can paraphrase the sentence,
217	identify the required action or decision, and explain any necessary specialized term without reading another artifact.
218	Rewrite it when the answer is no.
219	
220	---
221	# User Request Scheduling
222	
223	## Guidance
224	
225	When a user request arrives during active work, acknowledge receiving it immediately. Classify it using the Intermediate
226	versus Terminal Goals rule.
227	
228	When the request relates to the current terminal goal, treat it as steering for the current work and apply it
229	immediately. An explicit request to stop, cancel, replace, or do work instead of the current goal is related steering
230	that changes the terminal goal; apply it immediately and retain or discard queued goals only as the user directs. When
231	the request is unrelated, append it to the queued goals after every request already queued; process queued goals
232	first-come-first-served after the current terminal goal completes.
233	
234	When translating a user request into a tool or workflow invocation, supply an optional limit, policy, or setting only
235	when the user explicitly provides it or the request identifies the project's documented default. Authorization to use a
236	capability does not authorize selecting its optional parameters. For example, create or resume a goal without a token
237	budget unless the user states one; pass a stated budget exactly.

# File Links

## Guidance

When a reader-visible response refers to a local file, use a Markdown link: `[Description](target)`. The description
must contain the target's filename and, when available, append a colon followed by its decimal line number, such as
`ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7`. When the response refers to different targets with the same filename, include the
smallest subset of each target's full path that lets the reader distinguish them; otherwise do not include a directory
in the description. The target may use the full available path. Before finalizing, reject a bracketed local-file label
such as `[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7]` unless it has the Markdown link target required by this rule; brackets alone
are not a link. Write the target immediately after `(` and before `)`, without leading or trailing whitespace.

---
# Intermediate versus Terminal Goals

## Guidance

For every workflow, name the terminal goal and the acceptance evidence that proves it. Classify plans, staging
artifacts, repairs, migrations, investigations, commits, recorded transitions, and verification as intermediate tasks
unless their evidence proves every terminal acceptance condition.

Record every required terminal gate and its required evidence before execution. Mark each gate passed, failed, unrun, or
explicitly excluded by the user; do not infer a passed state from a related check. A failed or unrun required gate is an
unmet terminal condition. A clean build, an inspected result, a repaired intermediate artifact, or an existing sequence
of commits cannot substitute for the gate that the workflow requires.

Match evidence to the claim each terminal gate makes. Evidence that establishes only an enabling condition—such as
installation, configuration, authorization, discovery, connection, initialization, or process start—may pass only an
availability gate. It cannot pass a behavior or outcome gate. For those gates, require evidence from the relevant
execution boundary that the required behavior ran and produced its required effect. When availability itself is the
terminal outcome, record availability as that gate's claim.

When new work arises, classify it before acting. It supports the current terminal goal unless the user explicitly
replaces or expands that goal. Record its own completion evidence separately. After it completes, re-evaluate the
unchanged terminal conditions and continue from the next unmet condition. Do not report completion, return control as
complete, or discard required follow-up work on intermediate evidence.

Treat a user instruction as a goal change only when it explicitly replaces or expands the requested terminal outcome. A
discovered prerequisite, failure, repair, workaround, or implementation detail does not change that outcome merely
because completing it is necessary to proceed.

Before an irreversible action that represents completion—such as committing, finalizing, publishing, or declaring a
workflow complete—record the user-authorized scope and compare it with terminal acceptance evidence. Every scoped item
must have completion evidence or an explicit user-authorized exclusion. A prior result may reduce the remaining scope
only when durable evidence proves it covered the same item under the same governing contract; a tidy-looking history, an
earlier status claim, or partial inspection is intermediate evidence, not proof. Otherwise continue across the full
authorized scope. Immediately before the terminal action or claim, repeat that comparison, including the recorded gate
states, and report remaining work instead of success when any item is unaccounted for or any required gate is failed or
unrun.

---
# Target Audience

## Guidance

Write every user response, prompt or rule file, source comment or Javadoc, command help text, and error message so its
intended reader can identify the relevant actor, input or state, action, result, and next decision without knowing this
project's vocabulary.

Prefer common precise language. Introduce a specialized or abstract workflow term only when it conveys a distinction
that common language loses; define it at its first reader-visible use in concrete terms. Do not define a term by
repeating it or replacing it with other undefined project terms. When a plain definition still needs workflow
vocabulary, add the shortest before-to-after example that shows the ordinary observable effect. For example, replace
“whole later correction commit” with “a later commit containing only changes that complete or correct one earlier
feature.”

Apply the same test to a new category, exception, boundary, or conclusion. It is unexplained when a reader must accept a
label such as “family”, “complete”, or “required” without being told which observable facts make it true and what
decision those facts require. Do not let an example or desired result define that boundary. At its first use, name the
actor, observable facts, acceptance evidence, and resulting decision; then check one meaningful analogous case and one
dissimilar case to ensure the wording states the shared condition rather than the example's label.

Do not use an internal state or compound relationship label as its own explanation in reader-facing prose. Name the
artifact or action it represents and why it matters. When the label conceals why an operation cannot work in a receiving
state, explain the smallest causal sequence before proposing a remedy: the original and receiving states, operation,
assumption missing from the receiving state, and observable result. Then create a version of the selected operation that
relies only on the receiving state and verify its intended result. When the workflow lacks that capability, say that the
workflow and tool need a feature to create and verify it; do not imply that the change is impossible.

When warning that a check, observation, or result cannot establish a conclusion, explain the failed reasoning as an
observable sequence. Name the check or observation, the conclusion it might lead the reader to draw, the inputs or cases
it leaves unexamined, and the resulting incorrect decision. Then state the replacement procedure: which artifacts or
inputs to examine, the comparison or decision to make, and the evidence that completes it. Do not say only that the
reader must not rely on, assume, or treat something as proof; that does not explain why it is insufficient or how to
obtain the missing evidence.

When explaining a diagnosis, do not replace observed evidence and its limited conclusion with an internal label such as
"the model-facing boundary." First name the producer, the artifact, the differing observed values, and the resulting
behavior in their causal order. Then state only what those observations establish. If the unobserved step that changes a
value is not yet known, say that it remains to be located and name the next check; do not assign it to a component merely
because it lies between two observations.

For example, a patch prepared after `addsValidation()` exists can rely on that unchanged nearby text. When an earlier
commit lacks the method, Git cannot locate the patch. Create a version relative to that earlier commit and verify it. Do
not lead with labels such as “source tree,” “destination tree,” “target-adapted,” “reconstruction,” or “context” unless
the reader has first been given this explanation or the term is immediately defined in it.

Do not explain ordinary, broadly understood technical terms unless the project gives them a specialized meaning.

Before finalizing prose, review the actual draft—not only these guidelines—for internal labels, compound relationship
labels, and unexplained workflow terms. For each one, either replace it with the concrete artifact, relationship, and
action it hides, or define it where it first appears. Then ask whether the intended reader can paraphrase the sentence,
identify the required action or decision, and explain any necessary specialized term without reading another artifact.
Rewrite it when the answer is no.

---
# User Request Scheduling

## Guidance

When a user request arrives during active work, acknowledge receiving it immediately. Classify it using the Intermediate
versus Terminal Goals rule.

When the request relates to the current terminal goal, treat it as steering for the current work and apply it
immediately. An explicit request to stop, cancel, replace, or do work instead of the current goal is related steering
that changes the terminal goal; apply it immediately and retain or discard queued goals only as the user directs. When
the request is unrelated, append it to the queued goals after every request already queued; process queued goals
first-come-first-served after the current terminal goal completes.

When translating a user request into a tool or workflow invocation, supply an optional limit, policy, or setting only
when the user explicitly provides it or the request identifies the project's documented default. Authorization to use a
capability does not authorize selecting its optional parameters. For example, create or resume a goal without a token
budget unless the user states one; pass a stated budget exactly.

summary:
## Findings

- **[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:6](/home/gili/cat/worktrees/v1.0/.cat/temp/review-matrix.P6wLi8/runs/claude-cat-design/claude/msoykxds-b1aon0imxz/project/.claude/worktrees/agent-ac599851cb576605a/src/main/java/example/ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java#L6) Download API exposes an eager-content representation**
  - **Evidence:** `download` exposes a `byte[]` result, requiring the full receipt to be represented as an in-memory value at the endpoint boundary.
  - **Consequence:** The endpoint contract couples receipt delivery to eager materialization, so it cannot express incremental transfer or make resource ownership and closure part of its abstraction.
  - **Correction:** Make the download abstraction stream file content to the HTTP response, such as through an `InputStream` or framework streaming body with deterministic resource closure, rather than returning a complete byte array.
